name: Central Mnong
world_status: statement found in an open source
sweep_summary: Central Mnong is not in the catalog. All five Glottolog title hits (two Aissen 2000 Jakaltek records, Hirschberg & Ward 1991, Spathas 2010, Jasinskaja et al. 2005) are keyword mis-assignments -- each Glottolog reference page carries lgcode 'Central Mnong [cmo] (computerized assignment from "anaphora")' -- and none concerns Mnong. The material already on file from the 2026-09-16 pass gives the real stress evidence: Butler 2014 (Cornell PhD, Ch. 3 on Central Bunong, pp. 110 and 133) shows acoustically that minor syllables are always unstressed and that sesquisyllables are disyllabic iambs, i.e. fixed word-final stress; Phillips 1973 (MKS 4, p. 120) speaks of the 'main stressed syllable'; Sidwell 2000 (PL 501, p. 40) states the South Bahnaric family rule that minor syllables are always unstressed. New this sweep: Blood 1976 (MKS 5, Eastern Mnong Rơlơm; fetched sources and scanned, silent on stress) and Brunelle, Đinh & Tạ 2025 (Phonetica, Eastern Mnong Râlâm, open access via PMC; §2.1.1 'the final stressed syllable... while the initial syllable, or presyllable, has a reduced inventory'). Still unobtained: Butler 2015 'Bunong' in the Brill Handbook (paywalled, high priority as the citable sketch), Butler 2015 De Gruyter chapter (paywalled), Vogel & Filippi 2006 (print), Bequette 2008 thesis, Blood 1966/1968 Proto-Mnong, Filippi 2000 ms.

new_statements.quote: [p.110] Because minor syllable vowels are always unstressed, they will undoubtedly be shorter than CVC vowels. [p.127] Because CʌCVC vowels are unstressed and are found in disyllabic words while CVC vowels are stressed, we expect the latter to be longer than the former, and indeed they are. [pp.133-134] These results, considered together, suggest that Bunong minor syllables are indeed syllables that are unstressed. This conclusion supports the hypothesis that word types which are commonly called sesquisyllables are in fact disyllabic iambs. ... sesquisyllables in Bunong should be reinterpreted as ordinary disyllables. [pp.21-22] the Bunong word /rʌbɨŋ/ 'gourd' ... Light-Heavy iamb: [(rʌ.ˈbɨŋ)]
new_statements.citation: Butler, Becky A. 2014. Deconstructing the Southeast Asian Sesquisyllable: A Gestural Account. PhD dissertation, Cornell University (Cornell eCommons hdl 1813/36006).
new_statements.second_reader_evidence: Opened (extracted text of the held Cornell eCommons PDF) and located every quoted passage: (1) 'Because minor syllable vowels are always unstressed, they will undoubtedly be shorter than CVC vowels' at txt line 5513, bottom of p.110 running onto p.111 (sec. 3.3 intro to the acoustic study); (2) 'Because CʌCVC vowels are unstressed and are found in disyllabic words while CVC vowels are stressed, we expect the latter to be longer than the former, and indeed they are' at line 6140, p.127; (3) 'These results, considered together, suggest that Bunong minor syllables are indeed syllables that are unstressed. This conclusion supports the hypothesis that word types which are commonly called sesquis…
new_statements.rule_in_words: Bunong words are monosyllables or (maximally) disyllabic iambs: stress/prosodic prominence is on the word-final (major) syllable; the initial minor syllable (Cʌ, CʌN or syllabic nasal) — and the first syllable of the few true disyllables such as /ko.raɲ/ 'lord' — is unstressed, short and reduced.
new_statements.secondary_stress: None mentioned (words are at most two syllables).
new_statements.exceptions: None to final prominence; the author notes a 'very small set' of true disyllables (/ko.raɲ/ 'lord', /ka.mɔk/ 'knee', /tʃa.lot/ 'fall over') whose unstressed first syllables allow more vowel qualities than minor syllables (p.106).
new_statements.domain_note: Word level (prosodic word = one iambic foot); data are words in a carrier-style elicitation from Central Bunong speakers in Mondulkiri, Cambodia; acoustic (duration/formant) evidence for the unstressed status of non-final syllables.
new_statements.identity_note: Butler 2014 describes the Central Bunong dialect as spoken in Mondulkiri Province, Cambodia (Bunong/Phnong = Central Mnong [cmo], cent1992); she notes the same Central dialect is spoken across the border in Vietnam. Phillips 1973 describes Central Mnong of Vietnam (Bu Nar, Preh, Dih Bri, Bu Dang) and explicitly excludes 'Darlac Mnong' (Rơlơm, Gar, Kuan, Chil = Eastern Mnong, east2333). The earlier scan's named source (Blood 1966/1976 on Mnong Rơlơm) concerns Eastern Mnong, not this language.

new_statements.quote: Not only are they shorter than monosyllabic nuclei, they often have a greater distribution in their acoustic realizations, which is likely due to their shorter duration, which in turn correlates with their lack of stress. These results, considered together, suggest that Bunong minor syllables are indeed syllables that are unstressed. This conclusion supports the hypothesis that word types which are commonly called sesquisyllables are in fact disyllabic iambs. [p. 133] Because minor syllable vowels are always unstressed, they will undoubtedly be shorter than CVC vowels. [p. 110]
new_statements.citation: Butler, Becky Ann. 2014. Deconstructing the Southeast Asian Sesquisyllable: A Gestural Account. PhD dissertation, Cornell University (hdl 1813/36006). Chapter 3, Bunong (Central Mnong, Mondulkiri, Cambodia).
new_statements.locator: §3.6.1 Summary of Results, p. 133 (PDF p. 152); supporting sentence §3.4, p. 110; general definition §1.3, p. 8
new_statements.reading: Central Mnong (Bunong) words are monosyllables, sesquisyllables (unstressed Cʌ-/CʌN- minor syllable + full major syllable) and a handful of disyllables; stress is fixed on the word-final major syllable and the initial minor syllable is never stressed, i.e. sesquisyllables are disyllabic iambs. Non-contrastive, right-edge (final) stress. Independently consistent with Phillips 1973 p. 120 ('main stressed syllable' = the word-final main syllable) and with the family-level statement in Sidwell 2000 p. 40 and the Eastern Mnong statement in Brunelle et al. 2025 §2.1.1.

sources.note: Treats Bunong words as maximally disyllabic iambs: the word-final (major) syllable is stressed/prosodically prominent, the initial minor syllable (Cʌ, CʌN, N̩) is 'always unstressed' (p.110); 'CʌCVC vowels are unstressed... while CVC vowels are stressed' (p.127); acoustic results 'suggest that Bunong minor syllables are indeed syllables that are unstressed... sesquisyllables are in fact disyllabic iambs' (pp.133-134); Bunong /rʌbɨŋ/ 'gourd' parsed [(rʌ.ˈbɨŋ)] (pp.21-22); the few true disyllables (/ko.raɲ/ 'lord') likewise have an unstressed first syllable (p.106). Also reports Vogel & Filippi…

sources.quote: Mnong stops at the beginning of the main stressed syllable are contrastively fortis or lenis; the fortis stops have a further voicing contrast.
sources.note: Only an implicit statement: the segment inventories are stated for the 'main stressed syllable', i.e. the word-final main syllable is the stressed one; no rule of placement beyond that. Consistent with Butler 2014.
